slide.title: The close moves from waiting to flowing

body.text: Close takes 12 days, and about seven of them are spent waiting. Balance-sheet accounts are reconciled after the month ends, eleven entities match intercompany balances by email, and controllers see most entries for the first time on day nine. Errors surface when they are most expensive to fix, and every late finding reopens work that was already signed off.
The calendar looks full, but most of it is waiting: for a reconciliation, for a match, for a reviewer.

Reconciliations happen during the month, intercompany balances match overnight, and review rules check entries as they post. Exceptions reach a named owner on day one, so the days at the end are for sign-off rather than discovery. The controller signs off on day five, and the finance team gets its calendar back.
The calendar gets shorter because the waiting is designed out, not because anyone works faster.

slide.title: Three groups change how they work

body.text: Controllers move from a single review on day nine to rolling review from day one. They see exceptions, not every entry, and sign off on day five.
Time shifts from checking entries to judging exceptions.
Accountants reconcile balance-sheet accounts during the month with one template. Exceptions go to an owner the same day, with the evidence attached.
Month-end becomes a review of work already done.
The shared-service team runs intercompany matching overnight and clears breaks each morning, replacing email threads across eleven entities.
Fewer breaks reach the controller at all.

slide.title: Sequence and ownership drive the gain

body.text: Most of the delay is waiting, so the fix is a change in sequence and ownership more than a change in tools.
Today review happens after the books are drafted. We move rules to the point of entry, so a bad accrual is caught by the person who posted it, with the context still fresh.
Every close task gets one owner, a due time and an escalation path. When a task slips, the controller sees it on day one rather than finding it on day nine.

slide.title: What changes for the controller

body.text: The controller's first morning
On day one the controller opens a single exceptions queue instead of a stack of spreadsheets. Each item shows the account, the amount, the likely cause and the person who owns the fix.

By the end of day two most items are cleared by the entity accountants. What remains are judgment calls: a reserve, a reclassification, a timing question. Those are the items a controller should spend time on.
Nothing waits for the end of the month to be looked at, so nothing arrives all at once.
Note
Pilot entities cleared exceptions in two days on average, against nine days before the pilot.

slide.title: Where the savings come from

body.text: Most of the savings come from work that stops, not work that speeds up.
Supporting detail
Manual intercompany matching, duplicate review and rework after sign-off account for most of the $4.2M run-rate saving. None of it needs a faster tool; it needs the work designed out of the process.
We size the saving from the close calendar for 14 business units, then validate each line with the entity controller before it enters the business case.

slide.title: Eight changes deliver the five-day close

body.text: Why it matters
A close that runs on rules
Close takes 12 days because work waits for people. We resequence it so entries are checked as they post.

body.p: One template and owner for every balance-sheet account.
Intercompany balances match overnight across eleven entities.
Controllers review entries as they post, not in one push on day nine.
Every close task has a named owner, a due time and an escalation path.
Flash results are ready on day three and the full package on day five.
Evidence is captured as work happens, so audit requests stop reopening the close.
One calendar for 14 business units, built backward from the day-five target.
Breaks reach the right owner the same day, with the supporting evidence attached.
